publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Elevators or lifts in this town have in most cases in the past been designed principally as a means of avoiding the climbing of stairs, and their utility as such was very well demonstrated recently by their absence owing to the strike. The engineer was given very little consideration in erecting the machine and was usually assigned some out-of-the-way place, possibly under staircases, in which to instal the machine. To-day the utility is better appreciated, and the design, speed, and capacity are carefully considered in relation to the number of passengers or weight of goods, speed, number of floors to be served, and number of stops. In America express lifts are largely used, travelling many floors at a high speed (600 or 700 feet per minute), and then running local for the rest of the trip. In this town no buildings warrant such a service, and our fastest machine is 340 feet per minute. This speed is too great for local work, but is a great time-saving factor in returning to the ground floor or answering a call when two or three floors have to be travelled. The local speed of the machine is about 250 feet per minute. The average speed for passenger lifts in this town is about 200 feet per minute, although there are many of 250 feet to 300 feet.

abstract: Mr. G. V. Adendorff then delivered it lecture on the subject of thunderstorms. He gave a brief account of the early investigations of such pioneers as Franklin, and dealt with the determining factors as to how thunderstorms are formed, such as the clouds, the atmosphere and atmospheric electrification. The formation of clouds and the electrification of the atmosphere was lucidly explained by the lecturer, and the various points raised in connection with the various directions of the winds associated with thunderstorms was followed with keen interest by the members of the Institute. The lecturer then dealt with various phenomena connected with the actual electrification of clouds and explained how by the coalescence of electrified drops of moisture uniting in rain drops, and ultimately a cloud, a very large potential is attained. Having led up to the actual electrification of clouds, the peculiar vagaries and different kinds of lightning were then discussed. By a series of most interesting experiments which Mr. Adendorff had arranged, with considerable trouble, the effect of points dissipating a static charge and their protective effect was most beautifully shewn by means of the Wemshurst machine. The lecturer also pointed out the difference between the lightning discharges resulting from the breaking down of the atmosphere through electric stress in the case of steady electric strain and sudden or impulsive stress, and the lecturer explained the circumstances of the existence of these two conditions. The lecturer was highly successful with his experiments, and in the case of the impulsive stroke it was shewn clearly how the stroke took the path of least resistance, which was generally the highest object, no matter whether that object was pointed or otherwise; and that points which proved protective against the lightning stroke from a steady stress, were ineffective in protecting the highest object from being struck by the impulsive lightning stroke. This was a point which appealed very strongly to the members of the Institute as bearing upon the important subject of lightning protection, which was finally dealt with by the lecturer, thus terminating what was undoubtedly a highly interesting and beneficial lecture.

abstract: The President: Custom hath it that the outgoing President shall deliver a valedictory address. Webster defines “valedictory” as “of or pertaining to a leave-taking; a parting address, etc.” In olden times certain Roman citizens of note, at some time or other in their careers (generally at the end) were fond of this sort of thing, and the addresses in many cases were “parting” and given under circumstances over which they had no control. Some of the addresses had to do with a nation, an army or a city, and, considering the times, were generally framed in language that breathed optimism in the highest degree. Even one of our should-be foundation members, Noah, of Ark fame, was a pronounced optimist. I am a bit rusty on history, but no pessimist that I know of has ever delivered a farewell or any other address that has ever aided progressive engineering effort.

abstract: The Vice-President: Before we pass on to the next item I have been reminded that I should have drawn your attention under “General Business” to the Electricity Bill now before Parliament. The Electricity Bill of 1922 was rather sprung upon us in South Africa. Last year the Government, through the Minister of Mines and Industries, was good enough to submit a Draft Bill to the Technical Societies, and other bodies interested, for their comments and suggestions. The Institution of Engineers and our Institute formed a Joint Committee, and we went very carefully into the clauses of the Draft Bill. Certain recommendations were made which were sent to Capetown, but the Bill was withdrawn entirely. I do not know whether our objections helped to throw the Bill out or not; but this year a new Bill was sprung upon us without notice — in fact, the Bill was down for the second reading in the House before the “Government Gazette” containing the Bill was in our hands in Johannesburg. However, owing to sending telegraphic protests to Capetown the Bill was sent to a Select Committee, which gave us an opportunity again of sending our recommendations to Capetown, The Council of your Institute formed with the Institution of Engineers a Joint Committee to again go into the new Bill. Probably some of you have studied this Bill, but it would take too long to discuss tonight the clauses in detail. From our point of view one of the bodies suggested under this new Act, viz., the Control Board, a body formed entirely of Government servants, was one clause to which we are objecting most strongly. The Joint Committee prepared their report, submitted it to their respective Councils, and Mr. Elsdon Dew and Mr. Otley are presenting it to the Select Committee, but we have not heard the result. Mr. Sankey, who went down on behalf of the Municipality of Johannesburg, may be able to tell us something to-night.

As the question of maintenance charges was brought forward by various speakers it will perhaps be interesting to quote the Milner Report further. Concerning a valve panel of 24 valves to deliver 120 K.W. to the aerial it says : "The annual consumption of valves by such a set working 24 hours every day without cessation would be, according to our information, between 36 and 108 per station." This refers to silica valves, and with reference to glass valves it says, "about four times as many would be needed for equipment and renewals." Further mention is made of the cost of the valves, glass being £15 and silica £60. The latter, however, can be repaired when burnt out at £20 per valve.

publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: In a mining district such as ours, where a large proportion of the engineers are either directly or indirectly connected with the mines, it is surprising to note how little the subject of signalling in the mines has been dealt with in technical papers. Perhaps it is because the importance of the signalling system is not realised to the extent it deserves. The development of railways would have been considerably retarded without the telegraph, and I need add no words to convince you that the same would apply to deep level mines if signalling arrangements had not been devised. The method most commonly used for signalling in mines before electrical signalling became more general, consisted of a knocker operated by a flexible wire rope, the “knocker-line.” As this arrangement can be installed by the miner or timberman and can be kept in order by them, the mining men here “hung on” to this system as long as possible. It certainly has the advantage of being simple and, if properly installed, it is reliable within certain limits of length of shafts, and last, but not least, it keeps the electrician out of the shaft, which is a consideration! However, since the Government mining regulations require two systems of signalling, one of which can be operated only by an authorised person, mining men here had to resort to electric signalling. The system most commonly used on these fields is shown in its simplest form on Fig. 1. This shows the arrangement for two compartments of a shaft, and it will be seen that four wires are required to be led down the shaft. It is now the general practice to use rubber-insulated, lead-covered and wire-armoured cable for this purpose, with suitable “Tee” boxes at the various stations. The general rule is to use 7/20 s.w.g. wire, although 7/18 s.w.g. is used on some properties. In come cases the battery wires are heavier than the compartment wires, With regard to the insulation, I have not. heard of any paper-insulated cable being installed for this purpose on the Rand, but, provided proper tee boxes and end boxes are installed, I do not see any reason why paper cable should not be used; but perhaps the discussion, which I trust will be a lively one, Will give me your opinion in this respect. If you take measurements of the voltages obtaining at the various points of your bell system, you will find that the drops are comparatively high and that voltages occur where they are not expected and where they may become troublesome. Looking at Fig. 1: if LP9 pull is operated, the voltage at the terminal of the LBS bell will be the lowest, and it will also be found that a potential difference exists at some of the right compartment hells; to get clear on this latter point particularly, I rigged up a number of bells as per Fig. 1, using resistance wire for the connections between the various stations, thus getting as near as possible to actual working conditions. Between the surface bells and the bells at the first level, resistance wires of 1.14 ohms each are connected, being the equivalent resistance of 1,000 ft. of 7/20 s.w.g. copper conductor. Between the other levels each connecting wire has a resistance of 0.342 ohms, being the equivalent of 300 feet of 7/20 s.w.g. cable. We thus have reproduced the conditions which would prevail on a four-wire signalling system with one bell on the surface for each of the two compartments, one each at No. 1 level, 1,000 feet below the surface, and one bell for each compartment at each subsequent level, each level being 300 feet apart (as far as the cable run is concerned). The batteries should be connected direct on to the two battery leads PC and BC in Fig. 1. If a switch is used, it should be locked to prevent unauthorised persons from disconnecting the battery. “Where primary cells are employed the internal resistance of the cells will limit the amount of current on a short circuit occurring and thus prevent anything happening to the connections, but where accumulators are used, unless these be of a type that can stand short circuiting, I consider that some current limiting device should be employed in preference to fuses, and a properly selected iron wire resistance will meet the case, which on a short circuit would heat up and increase in resistance. Coming now to the pulls, there are a large number of different designs on the market and a good many different designs are in actual use on the Rand. I have not seen a pull yet which could not be improved in some way or another. Generally speaking, the bell pulls on the Rand can be divided into two classes : the side lever and the plunger type. The experience with the side lever is that the knife which makes contact by bridging the two contact springs wears badly, and after a while is apt to give two signals for one pull at the lever. The plunger type pull is theoretically of wrong design, as its action is that of an air-pump and is therefore liable to become dirty inside and corrode at the contacts, but in practice, however, this pull is generally found to be satisfactory. I have laid on the table a pull which was made to my design. This pull is intended to work in oil and you will notice has a quick make and break to ensure positive signals. As the law requires two distinct systems of signalling to be installed in each shaft, one which can be operated by an authorised person only and the otherby anyone from any level in the shaft, numerous lock bell pulls have been designed of late to meet this requirement. Some mines prefer ordinary bell pulls fitted in locked-up boxes which can be opened only by the properly authorised person, The lock bell pulls may have an attachment fitted to them which either locksthem mechanically or makes an electical disconnection. Another method is to have a separate electrical lock switch which is, in effect, the same as the last mentioned arrangement. Instead of having two complete separate systems, one for the call system and the other for the lock system, it is possible to combine the two systems by providing one additional to each compartment, and even this number can be reduced again by having an extra P.C. or pull common lead run down the shaft (Plumb's system); in the latter system the bells are common to both, but the driver has an indicator placed before him which is connected in series with the additional pull common leads. Because of the comparatively excssive drops, I would not advocate the use of common battery leads for more than two compartments, and for the same reason I think two complete separate systems are preferable, one for calling and the other for actual signalling. Whether a call system is installed with separate bells and pulls for each compartment, or with one bell and pull common to all compartments, is a question which must be decided in each particular case. I am under the impression that the regulations are met by providing a locked system for each working compartment and one call bell system or telephone system common to all compartments. In our further considerations it may be assumed that the Fig. 1 is that of a locked pull system.
